questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14082094/assets/f74f28bf0b5bf2208b3cebf837c667cf9a9ae737d7eb758708a98548ffca8e3a.png)

Which of the following gives the length of the curve $y=4{sin}^{2}⁡x$ on $[-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}],$ as shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=4{sin}^{2}⁡x,$ $a=-\frac{\pi }{2},$ and $b=\frac{\pi }{2}.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=4\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)
$$

Substituting ${f}^{′}(x)=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)$ into the arc length formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{1+{[{f}^{′}(x)]}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{1+16{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following gives the length of the curve $y=2\sqrt{x}$ on $[0,1]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=2\sqrt{x},$ $a=0,$ and $b=1.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{2}{2\sqrt{x}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}
$$

Substituting ${f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}$ into the arc length formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+{[{f}^{′}(x)]}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{\frac{1+x}{x}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Arc Length of a Smooth Curve Using the Arc Length Formula
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x),$ $a=1,$ and $b=3.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{x}{4}-\frac{1}{x}
$$

Now, let's compute $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}} & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x}{4}-\frac{1}{x})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+(\frac{{x}^{2}}{16}-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{2}}{16}+\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{4}+8{x}^{2}+16}{16{x}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{({x}^{2}+4)^{2}}{16{x}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{4x}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}=\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{4x}$ into the arc length formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(\frac{x}{4}+\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}+\operatorname{ln}⁡x)|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =[\frac{{3}^{2}}{8}+\operatorname{ln}⁡3]-[\frac{{1}^{2}}{8}+\operatorname{ln}⁡1] \\  & =1+\operatorname{ln}⁡3.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Compute the arc length of $y=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x})$ for $x\in [0,\operatorname{ln}⁡2].$
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}),$ $a=0,$ and $b=\operatorname{ln}⁡2.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x})
$$

Now, let's compute $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}} & =\sqrt{1+{[\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x})]}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4}({e}^{2x}-2+{e}^{-2x})} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}({e}^{2x}+2+{e}^{-2x})} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}{({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x})\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x})$ to the formula for the arc length, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}){|}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[({e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡2})-({e}^{0}-{e}^{-0})] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[2-\frac{1}{2}-0] \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Compute the arc length of $y=\frac{1}{8}{x}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ for $x\in [1,4].$
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\frac{1}{8}{x}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡x,$ $a=1,$ and $b=4.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{4}x-\frac{1}{x}
$$

Now, let's compute $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}} & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{1}{4}x-\frac{1}{x})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{16}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{16}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+\frac{16}{{x}^{2}}+8} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{(\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}=\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{4x}$ into the arc length formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{x}{4}+\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{1}{8}{x}^{2})|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)+\frac{1}{8}(4)^{2}]-[\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+\frac{1}{8}(1)^{2}] \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡4+2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\frac{1}{8} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡4+\frac{15}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\frac{2}{3}(x-3)^{3/2},$ $a=3,$ and $b=6.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{3}{2}(x-3)^{1/2}=\sqrt{x-3}
$$

Now, let's compute $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}} & =\sqrt{1+{[\sqrt{x-3}]}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+(x-3)} \\  & =\sqrt{x-2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}=\sqrt{x-2}$ to the formula for the arc length, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{3}^{6}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{6}\sqrt{x-2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{2}{3}(x-2)^{3/2})|}_{3}^{6} \\  & =[\frac{2}{3}(6-2)^{3/2}]-[\frac{2}{3}(3-2)^{3/2}] \\  & =\frac{16}{3}-\frac{2}{3} \\  & =\frac{14}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The length of a curve $y=f(x)$ is given by ${\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.$ Which of the following could be  an equation for this curve?
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We're given that 

$$
L={\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Comparing the above with the arc length formula, we see that we must have

$$
[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}=\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}\,⟹\,{f}^{′}(x)=\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}.
$$

Integrating the above equation with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\pm \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}\text{ d}x \\  & =\pm \operatorname{arcsin}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given options, the only one that has the required form is $y=\sqrt{2}-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x.$

The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that 

$$
L={\int }_{0}^{5}\sqrt{1+9{e}^{4x}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Comparing the above with the arc length formula, we see that we must have

$$
[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}=9{e}^{4x}\,⟹\,{f}^{′}(x)=\pm 3{e}^{2x}.
$$

Integrating the above equation with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\pm 3\int {e}^{2x}\text{ d}x \\  & =\pm \frac{3}{2}{e}^{2x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given options, the only one that has the required form is $y=\frac{3}{2}{e}^{2x}+1.$

canonical_examples.problem: What is the arc length of the curve $y = \arccos{x}$ on $\left[0,\dfrac{1}{2}\right]?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L = \int _a^b \sqrt{1 + [f'(x)]^2} \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)= \arccos{x} ,$ $a=0,$ and $b=\dfrac{1}{2}.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x)\mathbin{:}$

$$
f'(x) =-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}
$$

Substituting $f'(x) = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$ into the arc length formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{1+{[{f}^{′}(x)]}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{\frac{1-{x}^{2}+1}{1-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{\frac{2-{x}^{2}}{1-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Compute the arc length of  the curve $y=x^{3/2}$ between the points $x=0$ and $x=\dfrac{4}{3},$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14082094/assets/4ed8b94a4fff3c22697264e467f955f2e51a62618d03295c4e4f38493bff2ced.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L = \int _a^b \sqrt{1 + [f'(x)]^2} \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)= x^{3/2},$ $a=0,$ and $b=\dfrac{4}{3}.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x)\mathbin{:}$

$$
f'(x) =   \dfrac{3}{2}x^{1/2}
$$

Now, let's compute $\sqrt { 1 + [f'(x)]^2 }\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1+{[{f}^{′}(x)]}^{2}} & =\sqrt{1+{[\frac{3}{2}{x}^{1/2}]}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{9}{4}x} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{4+9x}{4}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}(4+9x)} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}}\sqrt{4+9x} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{4+9x}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\sqrt { 1 + [f'(x)]^2 } = \dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{4 + 9x}$ to the formula for the arc length, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+{[{f}^{′}(x)]}^{2}}\,dx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\frac{4}{3}}\sqrt{4+9x}\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate this integral using the substitution $u= 4+9x.$ Then, $\textrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{9}\textrm{d}u.$

We also need to compute new limits:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & \frac{4}{3} \\ u & 4 & 16\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\frac{4}{3}}\sqrt{4+9x}\,dx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{4}^{16}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{9}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{18}{\int }_{4}^{16}{u}^{\frac{1}{2}}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{18}{[\frac{2}{3}{u}^{\frac{3}{2}}]}_{4}^{16} \\  & =\frac{1}{18}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{[{u}^{\frac{3}{2}}]}_{4}^{16} \\  & =\frac{1}{27}([(16)^{\frac{3}{2}}]-[(4)^{\frac{3}{2}}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{27}([64]-[8]) \\  & =\frac{56}{27}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
The length of a curve $y=f(x)$ is given by ${\displaystyle  \int_{5}^{6} } \sqrt{1+\dfrac {x^2}{x^2-16}}  \,\textrm{d}x.$ Which of the following could be  an equation for this curve? 

- $y=  \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2-16}}$

- $y=  \sqrt{x^2-16} + \sqrt 5$

- $y=  \dfrac{x}{x^2-16} + 1$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L = \int _a^b \sqrt{1 + [f'(x)]^2} \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

We're given that 

$$
L=\int_{5}^{6}  \sqrt{1+\dfrac {x^2}{x^2-16}}  \,\textrm{d}x.
$$

Comparing the above with the arc length formula, we see that we must have

$$
[f'(x)]^2=\dfrac {x^2}{x^2-16}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f'(x) = \pm \dfrac {x}{\sqrt{x^2-16}}.
$$

Integrating the above equation with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\pm \int \frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-16}}\text{ d}x \\  & =\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}-16}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given options, the only one that has the required form is $y=  \sqrt{x^2-16} + \sqrt 5.$
